newsitem.title: UK: Russia unlikely to step up grain imports in 97/98.
newsitem.headline: Russia unlikely to step up grain imports in 97/98.

text.p: Russian demand for imported grain is unlikely to increase sharply in the 1997/98 season, mostly because its cattle and poultry numbers are still declining, the chairman of the Russian Grain Union, an association of local grain traders, said on Thursday.

"Considering that the number of cattle and poultry continues to drop, that it has not started to grow and there are no real grounds for believing that it will, there is no basis for increasing grain imports to Russia in the 1997/98 agricultural year," Alexander Yukish told the annual meeting of the International Grains Council.
Russia imported around four million tonnes of grain, including over two million tonnes of wheat, in the 1996/97 season.
Commenting on Russian export prospects, Yukish said the only possibilities were for sunflower, rye and barley and "very small quantities" of buckwheat and oats.
He also said Grain Union analysts did not expect any sizeable increase in grain exports from Russia in the next few years, adding that the same was true for imports.
Total Russian grain output is expected to reach 70 million tonnes in 1997, including 30 million tonnes of wheat, seven million tonnes of rye and 16 million tonnes of barley, he said.
In 1996 total output was 69.3 million tonnes, with 34.9 million tonnes of wheat, 5.9 million tonnes of rye and 15.9 million tonnes for barley.
